topics.name: Amino acids
topics.kicker: Building blocks of proteins · Twenty kinds spelled out by the genetic code
topics.dates: First one found in asparagus juice, 1806
topics.briefing: Amino acids are the small building blocks that link together, like beads on a necklace, to make every protein in your body, from the keratin in your hair to the enzymes that digest your lunch. Living things use 20 main kinds, and the order they are strung in is spelled out by the genetic code in DNA. Your body can make some of them, but nine, called essential amino acids, have to come from food.
topics.answerHtml: Amino acids (accept amino acid; prompt on acids; do not accept “proteins” or “peptides”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Forensic scientists spray ninhydrin [“nin-HY-drin”] on paper to reveal fingerprints, because it turns purple when it reacts with these molecules left behind in sweat. Ribosomes join these molecules into long chains using peptide bonds.
tossups.r: Each one has a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, and a side chain. For 10 points, name these building blocks of proteins.

tossups.p: In a famous 1950s experiment, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey sent electric sparks through a flask of methane, ammonia, hydrogen, and water vapor and produced several of these molecules. The simplest of these molecules, glycine, has just a hydrogen atom as its side chain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules that are joined by peptide bonds to build proteins.

tossups.p: The Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969, contained dozens of kinds of these molecules, including many that living things on Earth never use. Living things build their proteins from 20 standard kinds of these molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules, each containing an amine group and a carboxyl group.

tossups.p: The first of these molecules ever discovered was isolated from asparagus juice in 1806, and William Cumming Rose discovered the last of the 20 common ones, threonine, in the 1930s. Rose also showed which of these molecules people must get from food.
tossups.r: Nine of them are called “essential” for humans. For 10 points, name these building blocks that ribosomes join together to make proteins.

tossups.p: Selenocysteine, which contains the element selenium, is sometimes called the 21st of these molecules, and pyrrolysine [“peer-oh-LY-seen”], used by some archaea, is called the 22nd. In a protein, the order of these molecules is called its primary structure.
tossups.r: Transfer RNA carries them to the ribosome. For 10 points, name these molecules that ribosomes link together with peptide bonds.

tossups.p: At a particular pH called the isoelectric point, one of these molecules carries no net charge, and in water at neutral pH, these molecules exist as zwitterions [“TSVIT-er-eye-unz”], with both a positive and a negative charge.
tossups.r: Their side chains, called R groups, can be polar, nonpolar, acidic, or basic. For 10 points, name these 20 kinds of molecules that make up proteins.

tossups.p: All of the 20 standard kinds of these molecules except glycine are chiral, and proteins in living things are built almost entirely from their L-forms, though D-forms do appear in bacterial cell walls. Three-base codons in messenger RNA spell out which of these molecules comes next in a protein.
tossups.r: Nine of them are essential in the human diet. For 10 points, name these building blocks of proteins, such as glycine and lysine.

tossups.p: In the 1950s, Vernon Ingram showed that sickle-cell disease comes from a single swap in hemoglobin, in which glutamic acid is replaced by valine. Both of those are examples of these molecules, each of which is spelled out by a three-base codon.
tossups.r: Their order in a protein is called its primary structure. For 10 points, name these molecules that are strung together to make proteins.

tossups.p: Without vitamin C, the body cannot properly modify proline, one of these molecules, in collagen, which can lead to scurvy. In collagen’s long chains, every third one of these molecules is glycine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules that join together through peptide bonds to make proteins like collagen and keratin.

tossups.p: In 1908, chemist Kikunae Ikeda traced the savory “umami” taste of seaweed broth to glutamate, a form of one of these molecules, and helped turn it into the seasoning MSG. Transfer RNA molecules carry these molecules to the ribosome, matching each codon with an anticodon.
tossups.r: Each has an amine group, a carboxyl group, and an R group. For 10 points, name these building blocks of proteins.

tossups.p: Edman degradation identifies these molecules one at a time by snipping them off the N-terminus end of a protein chain. Frederick Sanger won the 1958 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for working out the order of these molecules in insulin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules, the building blocks of proteins, that ribosomes link with peptide bonds.

tossups.p: Tryptophan, one of these molecules, is the raw material the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin, and it is often wrongly blamed for sleepiness after a turkey dinner. Tyrosine, another of these molecules, is used to make dopamine and adrenaline.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules, 20 kinds of which build the proteins in your body.

tossups.p: Diet sodas sweetened with aspartame carry a warning for people with PKU, an inherited condition in which the body cannot break down phenylalanine, one of these molecules. Aspartame itself is made from two of these molecules, aspartic acid and phenylalanine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these building blocks of proteins, such as glycine and alanine.

tossups.p: Sixty-one of the 64 codons in the genetic code stand for these molecules, while the other three are stop signals. The codon AUG stands for methionine, which is usually the first of these molecules in a new protein.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these molecules, which transfer RNA carries to ribosomes to be built into proteins.

tossups.p: Cysteine, one of these molecules, contains sulfur and can form disulfide bridges that hold the keratin in hair in shape, which is why hair perms work by breaking and re-forming those bonds. When two of these molecules join, a water molecule is released.
tossups.r: Your body cannot make nine of them. For 10 points, name these building blocks of proteins, linked by peptide bonds.

clues.t: The building blocks (monomers) of proteins
Living things build their proteins from 20 standard kinds
Linked by peptide bonds into chains called polypeptides
Nine are “essential” for humans: the body cannot make them, so they must come from food
Each has a central carbon bonded to an amine group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a side chain (R group)
Glycine is the simplest: its side chain is a single hydrogen atom
Joining two of them is a dehydration (condensation) reaction that releases a water molecule
The genetic code uses three-base codons: 61 of the 64 codons stand for them, and three are stop codons
Transfer RNA (tRNA) carries them to the ribosome, matching its anticodon to a codon
Their order in a protein is called its primary structure
The start codon AUG stands for methionine, usually the first one in a new protein
Their R groups can be nonpolar, polar, acidic, or basic, which affects how a protein folds
Cysteine contains sulfur and forms disulfide bridges that hold the keratin in hair in shape
Tryptophan is used to make serotonin and melatonin; tyrosine is used to make dopamine and adrenaline
The Miller–Urey experiment (1950s) made several of them by sparking methane, ammonia, hydrogen, and water
At neutral pH they exist as zwitterions, with both a positive and a negative charge; at the isoelectric point the net charge is zero
Of the 20 standard ones, all but glycine are chiral; proteins use L-forms, but D-forms appear in bacterial cell walls
The Murchison meteorite (Australia, 1969) carried dozens of kinds, many never used by life on Earth
Asparagine, isolated from asparagus juice in 1806, was the first one discovered
William Cumming Rose discovered threonine, the last of the 20 common ones, in the 1930s
Selenocysteine (containing selenium) and pyrrolysine are sometimes called the 21st and 22nd
Ninhydrin turns purple when it reacts with them, revealing fingerprints on paper
Kikunae Ikeda traced umami, the savory taste of seaweed broth, to glutamate in 1908; it became the seasoning MSG
Frederick Sanger worked out their order in insulin and won the 1958 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Edman degradation removes and identifies them one at a time from a protein’s N-terminus
Vernon Ingram showed that sickle-cell disease comes from one swap in hemoglobin: glutamic acid replaced by valine
Vitamin C is needed to modify proline in collagen, which prevents scurvy; every third one in collagen is glycine
People with PKU cannot break down phenylalanine, so aspartame, made from aspartic acid and phenylalanine, carries a warning

trap.title: Links, not chains
trap.body: Many clues describe what these molecules build, like enzymes, keratin, collagen, or insulin, so players blurt “proteins.” But proteins are the long, folded chains, and these molecules are the single links. Nucleotides are the other trap: they are the building blocks of DNA and RNA, and clues about codons and the genetic code involve both kinds of molecules.
trap.fix: If the question wants monomers, “building blocks,” or molecules with an R group and an amine group, say amino acids. A folded chain or a named molecule like hemoglobin means a protein; a sugar, a phosphate, and a base mean nucleotides; long carbon tails in fats mean fatty acids.
trap.line: Real answer line: Amino acids (accept amino acid; prompt on acids; do not accept “proteins” or “peptides”)

topics.name: Cancer
topics.kicker: Disease of cells dividing out of control · Can spread through the body
topics.dates: Named for the crab by Hippocrates, c. 400 BCE
topics.briefing: Cancer is the name for more than 100 diseases that start the same way: changes in a cell’s genes make it divide out of control instead of following the body’s normal signals. The extra cells can pile up into a lump called a tumor and sometimes spread to other parts of the body. The ancient Greek doctor Hippocrates named it after a crab, and doctors treat many types with surgery, radiation, and medicines.
topics.answerHtml: Cancer (accept malignant tumors or malignant neoplasms; prompt on tumors or neoplasms)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Greek doctor Galen used a word meaning “swelling” for the growths caused by this disease, and that word’s root now names the medical specialty that treats it, oncology. Earlier, Hippocrates named this disease after a crab, possibly because a tumor’s spreading, finger-like edges reminded him of one.
tossups.r: Its cells can spread through the body. For 10 points, name this disease in which abnormal cells divide out of control.

tossups.p: Cells taken from a tumor of Henrietta Lacks in 1951, without her knowledge, became HeLa [“HEE-lah”] cells, the first human cells that could keep dividing in a lab indefinitely. Rebecca Skloot told the story of those cells and her family in _The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks_.
tossups.r: Unlike normal cells, cells of this disease ignore signals to stop dividing. For 10 points, name this disease, whose types include leukemia and melanoma.

tossups.p: In 1911, Peyton Rous showed that a cell-free extract from a chicken’s tumor could cause the same disease in healthy chickens, and he won a Nobel Prize for that work in 1966. Genes that push cells to divide too much and help cause this disease are called oncogenes.
tossups.r: Tumor suppressor genes normally act as brakes against it. For 10 points, name this disease in which cells grow uncontrollably and may form tumors.

tossups.p: In 1775, surgeon Percivall Pott linked a high rate of this disease among London’s chimney sweeps to soot, the first time it was tied to a job. Substances that cause this disease, like asbestos and chemicals in tobacco smoke, are called carcinogens.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease that is often treated with chemotherapy, radiation, or surgery.

tossups.p: The protein p53, nicknamed the “guardian of the genome,” stops damaged cells from dividing, and its gene is mutated in about half of all cases of this disease. Genes like BRCA1 also normally act as brakes against this disease.
tossups.r: Those brakes are called tumor suppressor genes. For 10 points, name this disease of uncontrolled cell division that can spread through the body.

tossups.p: Alfred Knudson’s “two-hit” hypothesis, based on retinoblastoma, a rare eye tumor in children, explained why both copies of certain genes must be damaged before this disease develops. Genes that cause this disease when they become overactive are called oncogenes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease in which cells divide uncontrollably and may spread to other organs.

tossups.p: The Philadelphia chromosome, made when pieces of chromosomes 9 and 22 swap places, causes a form of this disease called chronic myeloid leukemia, which the drug imatinib, sold as Gleevec, targets. Leukemia is a form of this disease that starts in the bone marrow.
tossups.r: Doctors who treat it are called oncologists. For 10 points, name this disease of uncontrolled cell growth.

tossups.p: Otto Warburg noticed that cells of this disease rely heavily on glycolysis to break down glucose, even when plenty of oxygen is around. Judah Folkman proposed that the tumors of this disease cannot grow large unless they recruit new blood vessels, a process called angiogenesis.
tossups.r: Doctors called oncologists treat it. For 10 points, name this disease in which abnormal cells divide out of control.

tossups.p: Cells of this disease often switch on telomerase, an enzyme that rebuilds the protective ends of chromosomes, so they can keep dividing far past the Hayflick limit, the usual cap of about 40 to 60 divisions for normal human cells.
tossups.r: When its cells spread to distant parts of the body, the process is called metastasis. For 10 points, name this disease in which cells divide out of control.

tossups.p: James Allison and Tasuku Honjo shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for finding ways to release the brakes on the immune system so it can attack cells of this disease, a treatment called immunotherapy.
tossups.r: Chemotherapy drugs fight this disease by killing fast-dividing cells. For 10 points, name this disease, which can form tumors that spread through the body.

tossups.p: In the late 1940s, Sidney Farber used the drug aminopterin to bring about the first temporary remissions in children with leukemia, a form of this disease, earning him the nickname “father of modern chemotherapy.”
tossups.r: Unlike benign tumors, the tumors of this disease can invade nearby tissue. For 10 points, name this disease in which abnormal cells divide out of control.

tossups.p: Siddhartha Mukherjee won the 2011 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for _The Emperor of All Maladies_, which he called a “biography” of this disease. Doctors who treat this disease are called oncologists.
tossups.r: Its name comes from the Latin word for “crab.” For 10 points, name this disease in which mutated cells divide uncontrollably, sometimes spreading through the body.

tossups.p: Canadian athlete Terry Fox, who had lost a leg to a bone form of this disease, set out in 1980 to run across Canada in a “Marathon of Hope” to raise money for research on it. Forms of this disease that start in bone or muscle are called sarcomas.
tossups.r: Melanoma is a form that starts in the skin’s pigment cells. For 10 points, name this disease in which cells grow out of control.

tossups.p: Bruce Ames developed a quick test that uses Salmonella bacteria to check whether a chemical causes mutations, which helps flag substances that might cause this disease. Carcinomas, the most common forms of this disease, start in cells that line the skin and organs.
tossups.r: Sarcomas start in bone or muscle instead. For 10 points, name this disease in which abnormal cells divide uncontrollably.

tossups.p: J. Michael Bishop and Harold Varmus won the 1989 Nobel Prize for showing that oncogenes come from normal genes, called proto-oncogenes, that help control cell growth. Damage to a cell’s DNA from things like ultraviolet light can start this disease.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this disease, which doctors often treat with surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.

clues.t: A group of more than 100 diseases in which abnormal cells divide out of control
Extra cells can form a lump called a tumor; benign tumors stay put, while malignant ones invade
Can spread to distant parts of the body, a process called metastasis
Treated with surgery, chemotherapy (medicines), radiation therapy, and immunotherapy
Hippocrates named it after a crab; its name is the Latin word for “crab”
Starts with mutations, changes in a cell’s DNA, which can be inherited or picked up during life
Carcinogens, such as ultraviolet light, asbestos, and chemicals in tobacco smoke, can cause it
Oncogenes push cells to divide too much; tumor suppressor genes normally act as brakes
Doctors who treat it are oncologists; Galen’s Greek word for “swelling” gave oncology its name
Carcinomas (the most common) start in linings of the skin and organs, sarcomas in bone and muscle, and leukemias in bone marrow
Melanoma starts in the skin’s pigment cells and is linked to ultraviolet light
Its cells avoid apoptosis, the programmed cell death that normally removes damaged cells
Its cells ignore cell-cycle checkpoints and contact inhibition, the signal that stops normal cells from dividing when crowded
The p53 gene, the “guardian of the genome,” is mutated in about half of all cases; BRCA1 is another brake gene
HeLa cells, the first human cells to divide indefinitely in a lab, came from Henrietta Lacks’s tumor in 1951 without her knowledge; Rebecca Skloot told her story
Peyton Rous showed in 1911 that a cell-free extract could pass a chicken tumor to healthy chickens; he won the Nobel Prize in 1966
Percivall Pott (1775) linked chimney sweeps’ high rate of it to soot, the first link to a job
Alfred Knudson’s “two-hit” hypothesis came from studying retinoblastoma, an eye tumor in children
The Philadelphia chromosome, a swap between chromosomes 9 and 22, causes chronic myeloid leukemia; the drug imatinib (Gleevec) targets it
Its cells rely on glycolysis even with oxygen around (the Warburg effect) and often switch on telomerase to keep dividing past the Hayflick limit
Judah Folkman proposed that tumors must recruit new blood vessels (angiogenesis) to grow large
James Allison and Tasuku Honjo won the 2018 Nobel Prize for immunotherapy that releases the immune system’s brakes
Sidney Farber, the “father of modern chemotherapy,” used aminopterin against childhood leukemia in the late 1940s
Siddhartha Mukherjee’s “biography” of it, _The Emperor of All Maladies_, won the 2011 Pulitzer Prize
Terry Fox, who lost a leg to a bone sarcoma, set out on his 1980 Marathon of Hope across Canada to raise money for research
The Ames test uses Salmonella bacteria to screen chemicals for mutations that might cause it
J. Michael Bishop and Harold Varmus (1989 Nobel Prize) showed that oncogenes come from normal proto-oncogenes

trap.title: Disease, not tumor
trap.body: A tumor is just a lump of extra cells. Benign tumors stay in one place and are not this disease; only malignant ones are, so an early buzz of “tumor” earns a prompt here instead of points. The word also has namesakes, like the crab constellation and zodiac sign and the Tropic of Cancer, which belong to astronomy and geography questions.
trap.fix: Say the disease’s name, not the lump. Uncontrolled cell division, metastasis, oncogenes, carcinogens, or chemotherapy point here; a constellation or a line of latitude points to astronomy or geography instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cancer (accept malignant tumors or malignant neoplasms; prompt on tumors or neoplasms)

topics.name: Mollusks
topics.kicker: Soft-bodied invertebrates · Snails, clams, squids, and octopuses
topics.briefing: Mollusks are soft-bodied animals, and many of them build hard shells to protect themselves: snails, clams, oysters, and scallops all belong to this huge group. Octopuses and squids are mollusks too, and they are among the smartest invertebrates on Earth, able to change color in a flash and squirt ink to escape. Most mollusks share a muscular foot and a skin-like mantle that makes the shell, and many scrape up food with a rough, toothy tongue called a radula.
topics.answerHtml: Mollusks (accept Mollusca or molluscs; do not accept a single class such as “cephalopods”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley shared a 1963 Nobel Prize for explaining nerve impulses, using a giant nerve fiber from one member of this phylum. Another member of this phylum, the sea hare Aplysia, helped Eric Kandel study how memories form.
tossups.r: Members of this phylum include squids and snails. For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals.

tossups.p: The Phoenicians crushed huge numbers of murex, members of this phylum, to make Tyrian purple, a dye so costly that it became the color of royalty. Many members of this phylum scrape up food with a radula [“RAJ-uh-luh”], a ribbon-like tongue covered with tiny teeth.
tossups.r: Most of its members have a muscular foot and a mantle. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes snails, clams, and octopuses.

tossups.p: As they develop, some members of this phylum twist their bodies 180 degrees in a process called torsion, which moves the mantle cavity and anus up over the head. Those members, the gastropods, are the largest class of this phylum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals that includes snails, slugs, and octopuses.

tossups.p: Chitons [“KY-tunz”], members of this phylum covered by eight overlapping shell plates, have teeth capped with the iron mineral magnetite. Bivalves are the only major class of this phylum that has no radula, the toothy, ribbon-like tongue that others use to scrape up food.
tossups.r: Its name comes from a Latin word meaning “soft.” For 10 points, name this phylum that includes octopuses and snails.

tossups.p: Engineer Marc Brunel based his tunneling shield for the Thames Tunnel on the shipworm, a wood-boring member of this phylum that damaged wooden ships for centuries. Clams, oysters, and mussels are members of this phylum with two hinged shells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals that also includes squids and snails.

tossups.p: Scallops, members of this phylum, can have up to 200 tiny eyes along the edge of their mantle, and each eye focuses light mainly with a curved mirror at its back. Like other bivalves in this phylum, scallops filter food from the water with their gills.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals that also includes snails, slugs, and squids.

tossups.p: The blood of some members of this phylum is blue because it carries oxygen with hemocyanin [“hee-moh-SY-uh-nin”], a protein that uses copper instead of iron, and the octopus pumps that blood with three hearts. Unlike most members of this phylum, cephalopods have a closed circulatory system.
tossups.r: Its members have a mantle and often a shell. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes octopuses, squids, and snails.

tossups.p: Extinct members of this phylum called ammonites are common index fossils, and the chambered nautilus, a living member with a similar coiled shell, controls its buoyancy with a tube called the siphuncle [“SY-fung-kul”]. Cephalopods in this phylum shoot water out of a siphon to jet away from danger.
tossups.r: Gastropods and bivalves belong to it too. For 10 points, name this phylum that includes octopuses, snails, and clams.

tossups.p: Like annelid worms, many members of this phylum begin life as a tiny swimming larva called a trochophore [“TROCK-uh-for”], and some then pass through a second larval stage called a veliger [“VEL-uh-jer”]. Members of this phylum have a mantle that can build a shell of calcium carbonate.
tossups.r: Clams and oysters belong to it. For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals that includes squids and snails.

tossups.p: Some members of the genus Conus in this phylum hunt fish by firing harpoon-like, venom-filled teeth, and a painkiller called ziconotide was developed from that venom. Gastropods, the largest class of this phylum, glide along on a single muscular foot.
tossups.r: Its members include slugs, clams, and octopuses. For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied invertebrates.

tossups.p: Some brightly colored sea slugs in this phylum, called nudibranchs [“NOO-dih-branks”], store the stinging cells of the sea anemones and other cnidarians they eat and use them for their own defense. Members of this phylum, from slugs to squids, have a fold of tissue called the mantle.
tossups.r: Its members have a muscular foot. For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied invertebrates that includes snails and clams.

tossups.p: In 1893, Kokichi Mikimoto produced the first cultured pearls by placing an irritant inside oysters, which coated it with layers of nacre [“NAY-ker”], or mother-of-pearl. Oysters belong to the class of this phylum called bivalves, which have two hinged shells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals that includes clams, snails, and octopuses.

tossups.p: Pet birds are often given cuttlebones, the internal shells of some members of this phylum, and the ink of those same animals gave its name to the reddish-brown color sepia. Octopuses and squids in this phylum change color using skin cells called chromatophores [“kroh-MAT-uh-forz”].
tossups.r: This phylum also includes snails, slugs, and clams. For 10 points, name this second-largest animal phylum, after the arthropods.

tossups.p: Zebra mussels, invasive members of this phylum that reached the Great Lakes in the late 1980s in ships’ ballast water, clog water intake pipes and crowd out native species. Members of this phylum called bivalves have two hinged shells held shut by strong adductor muscles.
tossups.r: Squids and snails are members too. For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals.

tossups.p: The colossal squid, the heaviest known invertebrate and a member of this phylum, has the largest eyes of any known animal. The study of animals in this phylum is called malacology, while the study of their shells is called conchology [“kong-KOL-uh-jee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phylum of soft-bodied animals that includes octopuses, snails, and clams.

clues.t: Phylum including snails, slugs, clams, oysters, squids, and octopuses
Its name comes from a Latin word meaning “soft”
Body plan: a muscular foot, a mass of internal organs, and a fold of tissue called the mantle
Many have a hard shell of calcium carbonate made by the mantle
The second-largest animal phylum, after the arthropods
Most scrape up food with a radula, a ribbon-like tongue covered with tiny teeth; bivalves have none
Main classes: gastropods (snails and slugs, the largest class), bivalves (clams and oysters), and cephalopods (squids and octopuses)
Bivalves have two hinged shells held shut by adductor muscles and filter food with their gills
Cephalopods are among the smartest invertebrates; they jet away by squirting water out of a siphon
Octopuses (eight arms) and squids (eight arms plus two tentacles) squirt ink and change color with chromatophores
Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood carrying copper-based hemocyanin; cephalopods have closed circulation, while most others have open circulation
Oysters make pearls by coating an irritant with nacre (mother-of-pearl); Kokichi Mikimoto first cultured pearls in 1893
Malacology is the study of these animals; conchology is the study of their shells
Gastropods twist 180 degrees as they develop (torsion), moving the mantle cavity over the head
Many start life as a trochophore larva, like annelid worms, and some then become veligers
Chitons have eight overlapping shell plates and teeth capped with the iron mineral magnetite
Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley used the squid’s giant nerve fiber (axon) to explain nerve impulses, winning a 1963 Nobel Prize
Eric Kandel studied how memories form in the sea hare Aplysia (2000 Nobel Prize)
The Phoenicians made Tyrian purple, the royal dye, from murex sea snails
Wood-boring shipworms inspired Marc Brunel’s tunneling shield for the Thames Tunnel
Scallops can have up to 200 eyes, each focusing light mainly with a curved mirror at its back
The chambered nautilus controls buoyancy with a tube called the siphuncle; extinct ammonites are index fossils
Some cone snails (genus Conus) harpoon fish with venom; the painkiller ziconotide was developed from it
Nudibranchs (sea slugs) store the stinging cells of the cnidarians they eat
Cuttlefish have an internal cuttlebone; their ink gave its name to the color sepia
Invasive zebra mussels reached the Great Lakes in the late 1980s in ships’ ballast water
The colossal squid is the heaviest known invertebrate and has the largest eyes of any known animal

trap.title: Phylum, not class
trap.body: Many clues describe just one class, like cephalopods for octopuses and squids, gastropods for snails, or bivalves for clams, and some tossups ask for those classes instead, so listen for “this phylum” versus “this class.” Brachiopods are the other trap: these “lamp shells” have two shells and look like clams, but they belong to a completely different phylum.
trap.fix: If the question asks for the phylum, or mixes clues about snails, clams, and squids, say mollusks. Arms, ink, and jet propulsion alone may mean cephalopods; two shells on the top and bottom (instead of left and right) mean brachiopods.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mollusks (accept Mollusca or molluscs; do not accept a single class such as “cephalopods”)

topics.name: Charles Darwin
topics.kicker: English naturalist · Explained evolution by natural selection
topics.briefing: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist who spent almost five years sailing around the world on HMS _Beagle_, collecting fossils, birds, and beetles and studying the giant tortoises and finches of the Galápagos Islands. Back home, he spent about 20 years building his theory of evolution by natural selection, which he finally published in 1859 in _On the Origin of Species_. He was born on the very same day as Abraham Lincoln: February 12, 1809.
topics.answerHtml: Charles Darwin (accept Darwin or Charles Robert Darwin; do not accept “Erasmus Darwin”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This scientist argued that ring-shaped coral atolls form when reefs keep growing upward around volcanic islands that are slowly sinking, an idea he published in an 1842 book. In 1835, he felt a major earthquake in Chile and saw that it had lifted the shoreline.
tossups.r: He later wrote _On the Origin of Species_. For 10 points, name this English naturalist who sailed aboard HMS _Beagle_.

tossups.p: This scientist spent about eight years studying barnacles, publishing a series of books about them in the 1850s. His theory was shaped by Thomas Malthus’s essay arguing that populations grow faster than their food supply, leading to a struggle for existence.
tossups.r: He described evolution by natural selection. For 10 points, name this author of _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: This naturalist and his shipmates accidentally ate part of a rare, smaller kind of rhea before he realized it was the bird he had been hunting for, and the species was later named after him. He also dug up fossils of giant ground sloths in Argentina.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who studied finches and tortoises on the Galápagos Islands during his voyage aboard HMS _Beagle_.

tossups.p: In 1837, this scientist sketched a branching tree beneath the words “I think” in one of his notebooks, and a similar branching diagram became the only illustration in his most famous book. He read Charles Lyell’s _Principles of Geology_ during his voyage around the world.
tossups.r: He explained evolution by natural selection. For 10 points, name this English naturalist who wrote _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: Joseph Hooker and Charles Lyell arranged for papers by this man and Alfred Russel Wallace to be read together at the Linnean Society in 1858, after Wallace mailed him an essay with the same idea. The next year, this man published his own book on that idea.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English naturalist who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection.

tossups.p: After studying a Madagascar orchid whose nectar sat at the bottom of a tube about a foot long, this scientist predicted that a moth with an equally long tongue must exist, and a moth matching his prediction was described in 1903.
tossups.r: He also wrote _The Descent of Man_, which described sexual selection. For 10 points, name this naturalist who sailed on HMS _Beagle_.

tossups.p: This scientist’s last book, published in 1881, described how earthworms slowly bury stones and build up soil. He worked for decades at Down House in Kent, where he did much of his thinking while walking a path he called the Sandwalk.
tossups.r: He proposed natural selection. For 10 points, name this author of _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: This scientist proposed that tiny particles called gemmules travel from every part of the body to carry traits to offspring, a mistaken idea he called pangenesis. He studied artificial selection by breeding fancy pigeons at his home.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English naturalist who published _On the Origin of Species_ in 1859.

tossups.p: In an 1860 debate at Oxford, Bishop Samuel Wilberforce clashed with Thomas Henry Huxley, who was nicknamed this scientist’s “bulldog” for defending his ideas. Herbert Spencer coined the phrase “survival of the fittest,” which this scientist later used in his own work.
tossups.r: He described evolution by natural selection. For 10 points, name this author of _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: In Argentina, this naturalist dug up fossils of giant ground sloths and armored glyptodonts [“GLIP-tuh-donts”] and noticed that they resembled smaller animals, like armadillos, that still lived there. During his voyage, he read Charles Lyell’s _Principles of Geology_.
tossups.r: Lyell’s book argued that Earth changes slowly over long ages. For 10 points, name this English naturalist who sailed on HMS _Beagle_.

tossups.p: This scientist ended his most famous book by describing an “entangled bank” full of life and declaring that “endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful” have evolved from simple beginnings. He called his idea “descent with modification.”
tossups.r: That book appeared in 1859. For 10 points, name this English naturalist who wrote _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: Botanist John Stevens Henslow recommended this young man as a companion for Captain Robert FitzRoy on a surveying voyage that left England in 1831. This man suffered badly from seasickness on that voyage, but he spent long stretches of it exploring on land.
tossups.r: That voyage took him to the Galápagos Islands in 1835. For 10 points, name this naturalist who sailed aboard HMS _Beagle_ and later wrote _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: This man’s grandfathers were the pottery maker Josiah Wedgwood and the doctor Erasmus, who wrote the book _Zoonomia_, and this man married his cousin Emma Wedgwood. He dropped out of medical school in Edinburgh.
tossups.r: He then studied at Cambridge to become a clergyman before sailing on HMS _Beagle_. For 10 points, name this naturalist who wrote _On the Origin of Species_.

tossups.p: The ornithologist John Gould told this scientist that the small brown birds he had collected on different Galápagos islands were separate species of finches. This man also learned that the islands’ mockingbirds and giant tortoises differed from island to island.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English naturalist who sailed on HMS _Beagle_ and proposed natural selection.

tossups.p: This scientist’s 1872 book _The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals_ used photographs to compare the faces people and animals make when they feel emotions. He is buried in Westminster Abbey, near Isaac Newton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this author of _On the Origin of Species_, who was born on the same day as Abraham Lincoln.

Sailed around the world as a naturalist on HMS _Beagle_ (1831–1836)

Read Charles Lyell’s _Principles of Geology_, about slow change over long ages, during the voyage

Dug up fossils of giant ground sloths and glyptodonts in South America, relatives of living sloths and armadillos
Died in 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey near Isaac Newton
Explained that coral atolls form as reefs grow upward around slowly sinking volcanic islands (1842 book); saw a Chilean earthquake lift the shoreline (1835)
Spent about eight years studying barnacles

trap.title: Not Wallace, not Lamarck
trap.body: Alfred Russel Wallace came up with natural selection on his own while exploring the Malay Archipelago, and their papers were read together in 1858, so some clues fit both men. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck had an older, wrong theory that living things pass on traits they gain by using their bodies, like a giraffe stretching its neck. And the doctor and poet Erasmus Darwin, author of _Zoonomia_, was Charles’s grandfather.
trap.fix: The _Beagle_, the Galápagos, barnacles, earthworms, or _On the Origin of Species_ mean Charles Darwin; the Malay Archipelago and the Wallace Line mean Wallace; use and disuse of body parts means Lamarck. If a clue could fit the grandfather, say “Charles Darwin” in full.
trap.line: Real answer line: Charles Darwin (accept Darwin or Charles Robert Darwin; do not accept “Erasmus Darwin”)

topics.name: Cholesterol
topics.kicker: Waxy steroid in animal cell membranes · Raw material for bile and hormones
topics.briefing: Cholesterol has a bad reputation, but your body can’t live without it. This waxy steroid is a key building block of the membrane around every animal cell, and your body turns it into bile acids and into hormones like testosterone and estrogen. Trouble starts when too much of it, carried through the blood by “bad” LDL particles, builds up as plaque inside artery walls.
topics.answerHtml: Cholesterol (prompt on sterol or steroid; do not accept “LDL” or “HDL”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: French chemist Michel Chevreul [“shuh-VRUHL”] named this substance in 1815, taking its name from Greek words meaning “bile” and “solid” because it was first found in solid form in gallstones. A related molecule in the skin is converted into vitamin D by ultraviolet light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this waxy steroid, carried in the blood by LDL and HDL, that can build up as plaque in arteries.

tossups.p: Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein shared the 1985 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the receptor that lets cells pull in particles carrying this substance. Faulty versions of that receptor cause an inherited condition in which blood levels of this substance are very high from birth.
tossups.r: Statin drugs lower levels of this substance. For 10 points, name this steroid found in animal cell membranes.

tossups.p: Konrad Bloch and Feodor Lynen won a 1964 Nobel Prize for working out how cells build this molecule, a process in which squalene [“SKWAY-leen”] is converted into lanosterol on the way to the final product. Its production starts from acetyl-CoA in the mevalonate [“meh-VAL-uh-nate”] pathway.
tossups.r: Egg yolks are rich in this molecule. For 10 points, name this lipid that is carried in the blood by LDL and HDL.

tossups.p: HMG-CoA reductase is the enzyme that sets the pace of this substance’s production in the body. Japanese biochemist Akira Endo found the first drug that blocks that enzyme in a mold, launching a family of widely used medicines.
tossups.r: Those drugs, the statins, lower its level in the blood. For 10 points, name this waxy steroid carried by “good” HDL and “bad” LDL.

tossups.p: In 1888, Friedrich Reinitzer [“RYE-nit-ser”] discovered liquid crystals while studying a benzoate made from this compound, which seemed to melt twice. A twisted liquid-crystal phase is still named for this compound, whose structure includes four fused rings and one hydroxyl group.
tossups.r: Statins lower blood levels of this compound. For 10 points, name this sterol that is found in animal cell membranes and can clog arteries.

tossups.p: This molecule packs together with sphingolipids [“SFING-go-lip-idz”] to form thicker, more orderly patches of membrane called lipid rafts. It also acts as a “fluidity buffer,” keeping animal cell membranes from becoming too runny when warm or too stiff when cold.
tossups.r: It is carried through the blood by LDL and HDL. For 10 points, name this steroid, made by the liver, that can build up as plaque inside arteries.

tossups.p: Many antifungal drugs target ergosterol, the sterol that fungi use in place of this one in their cell membranes. Plants use similar molecules called phytosterols, so plant foods contain almost none of this compound, which is common in egg yolks and meat.
tossups.r: High blood levels of it are treated with statins. For 10 points, name this steroid carried through the blood by LDL and HDL particles.

tossups.p: Inside mitochondria, an enzyme snips off part of this molecule’s side chain to make pregnenolone [“preg-NEE-nuh-lohn”], the first step in making cortisol, aldosterone, and other steroid hormones. The liver also converts this molecule into bile acids, which are stored in the gallbladder as part of bile.
tossups.r: LDL particles carry it to body cells. For 10 points, name this lipid whose high blood levels are linked to heart disease.

tossups.p: White blood cells called macrophages can swallow so many particles carrying this substance that they swell into “foam cells” inside artery walls. Those cells help form the fatty plaques of atherosclerosis [“ath-uh-roh-skluh-ROH-sis”], which can narrow arteries and lead to heart attacks.
tossups.r: Egg yolks are a rich source of it. For 10 points, name this waxy steroid that “bad” LDL particles carry through the blood.

tossups.p: This compound has 27 carbon atoms, and its four fused rings are labeled A through D, with the D ring holding only five carbons. A hydroxyl group on carbon 3 makes it a sterol, and that small polar end points toward the water at the surface of a cell membrane.
tossups.r: Too much of it can form plaque in arteries. For 10 points, name this molecule whose blood levels are lowered by statins.

tossups.p: A molecule that differs from this one by just one extra double bond is turned into vitamin D when ultraviolet light strikes the skin. Many gallstones are made mostly of this compound, which is also the raw material for testosterone and estrogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this steroid found in animal cell membranes and carried in the blood by LDL.

tossups.p: In a process called reverse transport, high-density lipoproteins collect extra amounts of this substance from body tissues and carry them back to the liver. Low-density lipoproteins carry it the other way, out to body cells, and high levels of them are linked to clogged arteries.
tossups.r: Statin drugs lower its levels. For 10 points, name this waxy steroid that is found in egg yolks and animal cell membranes.

tossups.p: Adolf Windaus [“VIN-douse”] won the 1928 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research on sterols like this one, and on how they connect to vitamins. The fatty myelin sheaths that insulate nerve fibers are especially rich in this lipid.
tossups.r: Egg yolks are among the richest food sources of it. For 10 points, name this substance carried in the blood by LDL and HDL.

tossups.p: Cholic [“KOH-lick”] acid, one of the two main bile acids made by the human liver, is built from this molecule. Bile acids help the intestine digest fats, and making them is one of the main ways the body gets rid of extra amounts of this molecule.
tossups.r: LDL carries it to body cells. For 10 points, name this steroid whose buildup in arteries can lead to heart disease.

tossups.p: Blood tests often report this substance’s total level along with separate numbers for its two main carriers, one nicknamed “good” and the other “bad.” Doctors may prescribe statins when its level is too high, since extra amounts can build up in artery walls.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this waxy steroid that is carried in the blood by HDL and LDL.

clues.t: A waxy, fat-like steroid that animal cells need to build their membranes
Carried through the blood by lipoproteins: LDL (nicknamed “bad”) and HDL (nicknamed “good”)
Too much in the blood can build up as plaque in artery walls and raise the risk of heart disease
Statin drugs lower its level in the blood
The body makes most of what it needs; in food it comes from animal products, such as egg yolks and meat
Four fused carbon rings plus one hydroxyl (–OH) group make it a sterol, or steroid alcohol
In animal cell membranes it acts as a “fluidity buffer”: not too runny when warm, not too stiff when cold
Raw material for steroid hormones like testosterone, estrogen, cortisol, and aldosterone
The liver turns it into bile acids, which are stored in the gallbladder as part of bile; this is a main way the body gets rid of it
Many gallstones are made mostly of it; its name comes from Greek words for “bile” and “solid”
A close relative with one extra double bond is turned into vitamin D when ultraviolet light hits the skin
Its buildup in artery walls is part of atherosclerosis, which can lead to heart attacks
Fungi use ergosterol in its place, and plants use phytosterols; many antifungal drugs target ergosterol
Especially plentiful in the myelin sheaths that insulate nerve fibers
French chemist Michel Chevreul named it in 1815, after it was first found in solid form in gallstones
Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein won the 1985 Nobel Prize for discovering the LDL receptor, which pulls it into cells
Faulty LDL receptors cause a familial (inherited) condition with very high blood levels of it from birth
Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that sets the pace of its production; Akira Endo found the first statin in a mold
Konrad Bloch and Feodor Lynen won the 1964 Nobel Prize for working out how cells build it
Built from acetyl-CoA through the mevalonate pathway; squalene and lanosterol are steps along the way
Making steroid hormones starts when an enzyme in mitochondria snips off part of its side chain to form pregnenolone
Cholic acid, one of the two main bile acids made by the human liver, is built from it
Friedrich Reinitzer discovered liquid crystals in 1888 while studying a benzoate made from it; a twisted liquid-crystal phase is named for it
Packs with sphingolipids into thick, orderly membrane patches called lipid rafts
In artery plaques, macrophages that swallow too much LDL swell into “foam cells”
Has 27 carbon atoms; its four rings are labeled A through D, and the D ring has only five carbons
In “reverse transport,” HDL carries extra amounts of it from body tissues back to the liver
Adolf Windaus won the 1928 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research on sterols like it and their link to vitamins

trap.title: The molecule, not its carriers
trap.body: LDL and HDL are not cholesterol itself. They are lipoproteins, tiny packages of fat and protein that carry it through the blood, but people call them “bad cholesterol” and “good cholesterol,” so players blurt “LDL” when a question wants the molecule. Others answer “steroid” or “sterol,” which names the whole family of four-ring molecules, not this one member.
trap.fix: If the question says “this molecule,” “this sterol,” or “this compound,” say cholesterol. Save “LDL” for a question about “this lipoprotein” that delivers it to cells, and “HDL” for the one that carries it back to the liver.
trap.line: Real answer line: Cholesterol (prompt on sterol or steroid; do not accept “LDL” or “HDL”)

topics.name: Retina
topics.kicker: Light-sensing layer at the back of the eye · Home of the rods and cones
topics.dates: Lines the back of the eye
topics.briefing: The retina is a thin sheet of tissue lining the back of each eye, and it is where seeing really begins. Millions of cells called rods and cones turn light into electrical signals that travel down the optic nerve to the brain. The eye’s lens projects an upside-down image onto it, and the brain makes sense of that image so the world looks right side up.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Alfred Knudson developed his “two-hit” hypothesis by studying a rare childhood cancer of this tissue that is linked to mutations in the RB gene. This tissue’s sharpest vision comes from a small central pit called the fovea [“FOH-vee-uh”].
tossups.r: It sends signals down the optic nerve. For 10 points, name this layer at the back of the eye that contains rods and cones.

tossups.p: Edme Mariotte [“mar-ee-OT”] discovered in the 1600s that one part of this tissue can’t detect light at all. That blind spot, the optic disc, has no light-sensing cells because it is where nerve fibers bundle together and exit the eye.
tossups.r: Elsewhere, its fovea gives the sharpest vision. For 10 points, name this light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.

tossups.p: George Wald shared a 1967 Nobel Prize for showing how vitamin A is used in this tissue. When light strikes it, a bent vitamin A–based molecule straightens from its “cis” shape into its “trans” shape, which starts a nerve signal.
tossups.r: This tissue’s cones detect color. For 10 points, name this layer at the back of the eye that sends signals down the optic nerve.

tossups.p: In this tissue, the G protein transducin [“trans-DOO-sin”] activates an enzyme that breaks down cyclic GMP, closing sodium channels. As a result, its light-sensing cells release less of the neurotransmitter glutamate when light hits them, and more in the dark.
tossups.r: Its central pit, the fovea, is packed with cones. For 10 points, name this layer of the eye whose rod cells contain the pigment rhodopsin.

tossups.p: In 1604, Johannes Kepler correctly explained that the lens of the eye focuses an image onto this tissue, and that the image arrives upside down. Most people have three kinds of color-sensing cells in this tissue, and a missing or faulty kind causes color blindness.
tossups.r: Its signals reach the brain through the optic nerve. For 10 points, name this light-sensitive layer that contains rods and cones.

tossups.p: Horizontal cells and amacrine [“AM-uh-krin”] cells link neurons sideways within this tissue. Light must pass through its layers of ganglion cells and bipolar cells before reaching the light-sensing cells at the very back, and the ganglion cells’ long fibers bundle together to form the optic nerve.
tossups.r: It contains rods and cones. For 10 points, name this layer of tissue at the back of the eye.

tossups.p: A small group of this tissue’s ganglion cells use the pigment melanopsin to sense brightness and help set the body’s daily clock, or circadian rhythm. Those signals travel to a part of the brain called the suprachiasmatic [“soo-pruh-kye-az-MAT-ik”] nucleus.
tossups.r: Its rods work in dim light, and its cones detect color. For 10 points, name this layer at the back of the eye.

tossups.p: This tissue grows out of the developing brain and folds into a cup shape, so scientists count it as part of the central nervous system. Its dark outermost layer, the pigment epithelium, soaks up stray light and helps recycle the vitamin A–based molecules its light-sensing cells use.
tossups.r: The optic nerve carries its signals to the brain. For 10 points, name this light-sensitive layer that contains rods and cones.

tossups.p: Hermann von Helmholtz’s 1851 invention, the ophthalmoscope [“off-THAL-muh-skope”], let doctors peer through the pupil and see this tissue inside a living eye. Eye doctors examine its blood vessels for damage caused by diabetes, and its vessel pattern is unique enough to identify a person in a security scan.
tossups.r: Its fovea is packed with cones. For 10 points, name this light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.

tossups.p: In cats and many other animals that are active at night, a mirror-like layer called the tapetum lucidum [“tuh-PEE-tum LOO-sih-dum”] sits behind this tissue and bounces light back through it, making their eyes shine in headlights. In humans, this tissue’s rods take over in dim light.
tossups.r: It sends signals through the optic nerve. For 10 points, name this layer at the back of the eye whose cones detect color.

tossups.p: Age-related macular degeneration damages the center of this tissue, blurring the middle of a person’s view. That central area, the macula, contains a tiny pit called the fovea [“FOH-vee-uh”], which is packed with cones and gives the sharpest vision.
tossups.r: The optic nerve carries its signals to the brain. For 10 points, name this layer at the back of the eye that also contains rods.

tossups.p: The pigment rhodopsin [“roh-DOP-sin”], once called “visual purple,” is packed into the rod cells of this tissue and is made from a protein called opsin plus a molecule built from vitamin A. Because of that, a lack of vitamin A can cause night blindness.
tossups.r: It lines the back of the eye. For 10 points, name this light-sensitive layer whose cone cells detect color.

tossups.p: Octopuses and squids have a version of this tissue with its light-sensing cells facing toward the light and its nerve fibers behind, so they have no blind spot. In humans, light must pass through layers of nerve cells in this tissue before reaching the light-sensing cells at the back.
tossups.r: Its signals leave the eye through the optic nerve. For 10 points, name this layer of the eye that contains rods and cones.

tossups.p: Santiago Ramón y Cajal [“kah-HAHL”] drew detailed pictures of the layers of neurons in this tissue. At dusk, reds start to look darker compared with blues, an effect called the Purkinje [“pur-KIN-jee”] shift, because this tissue’s rods take over from its cones.
tossups.r: It sends signals to the brain through the optic nerve. For 10 points, name this light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.

tossups.p: This tissue turns light into electrical signals using two kinds of cells: one kind works best in dim light, and the other kind needs brighter light and detects color. The lens of the eye focuses an upside-down image onto this tissue.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer at the back of the eye that sends signals down the optic nerve.

clues.t: Thin, light-sensitive layer of tissue lining the back of the eye
Contains the light-sensing cells called rods and cones
Sends its signals to the brain through the optic nerve
The eye’s lens focuses an upside-down image onto it
Rods work in dim light (night vision); cones need brighter light and detect color
Most people have three kinds of cones, most sensitive to red, green, or blue light; a missing or faulty kind causes color blindness
The fovea, a small central pit packed with cones, gives the sharpest vision
The fovea sits in the macula, the central area damaged in age-related macular degeneration
The optic disc, where nerve fibers exit the eye, has no light-sensing cells and creates a blind spot
Rods are packed with the pigment rhodopsin (“visual purple”), made of the protein opsin plus a vitamin A–based molecule
A lack of vitamin A can cause night blindness, because rods need it to make their pigment
Light passes through layers of ganglion cells and bipolar cells before reaching the rods and cones at the back; ganglion cell fibers form the optic nerve
Eye doctors check its blood vessels for damage from diabetes; the vessel pattern is unique enough for security scans
Octopus and squid versions have light-sensing cells facing the light, with nerve fibers behind, so they have no blind spot
Edme Mariotte discovered its blind spot in the 1600s
Johannes Kepler explained in 1604 that the lens focuses an upside-down image onto it
George Wald shared a 1967 Nobel Prize for showing how vitamin A works here: light straightens a bent molecule from its “cis” to its “trans” shape
The G protein transducin triggers the breakdown of cyclic GMP, so its light-sensing cells release less glutamate in light and more in the dark
Horizontal cells and amacrine cells connect its neurons sideways
A rare childhood cancer of this tissue, linked to the RB gene, led Alfred Knudson to his “two-hit” hypothesis
Grows out of the developing brain and folds into a cup, so it counts as part of the central nervous system
Some of its ganglion cells use melanopsin to sense brightness and set the body’s circadian rhythm, signaling the suprachiasmatic nucleus
Its dark outermost layer, the pigment epithelium, absorbs stray light and recycles vitamin A–based molecules
Hermann von Helmholtz invented the ophthalmoscope in 1851, letting doctors see it inside a living eye
In cats, a mirror-like layer behind it, the tapetum lucidum, bounces light back through it and makes their eyes shine
Santiago Ramón y Cajal drew detailed pictures of its layers of neurons
The Purkinje shift: at dusk its rods take over from its cones, so reds look darker compared with blues

trap.title: The layer, not its parts
trap.body: Many tossups on this tissue describe its parts, like the fovea, the rods and cones, or the blind spot, and players blurt out the part instead of the whole layer. Others hear “vitamin A” or “cis and trans” and answer “retinal,” which is the light-catching molecule inside rhodopsin and a different answer line. The cornea and lens focus light; they don’t sense it.
trap.fix: If the question says “this tissue,” “this layer,” or “this structure at the back of the eye,” say retina. Save “fovea” for “this central pit,” “optic disc” for “this blind spot,” and “retinal” for a question about “this molecule.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Retina (accept retinas or retinae; do not accept “retinal”)

topics.name: Gregor Mendel
topics.kicker: Austrian monk who bred pea plants · Discovered the basic laws of heredity
topics.briefing: Gregor Mendel was a monk who spent about eight years in his monastery’s garden in Brno crossing tens of thousands of pea plants. By counting how traits like seed color and flower color showed up in each generation, he discovered the basic rules of heredity. Almost nobody paid attention until 1900, 16 years after his death, when three scientists rediscovered his work and he became known as the “father of genetics.”
topics.answerHtml: Gregor Mendel (accept Gregor Johann Mendel; do not accept “Mendeleev”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1936, statistician Ronald Fisher argued that this scientist’s data fit his predicted ratios suspiciously well, seeming almost too good to be true. This man’s 1866 paper “Experiments on Plant Hybridization” was largely ignored for more than 30 years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Austrian monk who discovered the basic laws of heredity by crossbreeding pea plants.

tossups.p: Botanist Carl Nägeli [“NAY-guh-lee”] encouraged this scientist to repeat his experiments on hawkweed, which gave confusing results because hawkweed can make seeds without fertilization. This man had first worked out his ideas during about eight years of growing plants in a monastery garden.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this monk whose experiments with pea plants made him the “father of genetics.”

tossups.p: Christian Doppler was one of this man’s physics teachers at the University of Vienna, which he attended after failing an exam to become a certified teacher. He later returned to St. Thomas’s Abbey in Brno [“BUR-noh”], where he ran his famous experiments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this monk who found a 3 to 1 ratio of traits by crossing pea plants.

tossups.p: In 1900, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak [“CHAIR-mahk”] each published results that matched this scientist’s forgotten work. William Bateson, who later coined the word “genetics,” became a leading champion of this man’s ideas in English.
tossups.r: He is called the “father of genetics.” For 10 points, name this monk who described dominant and recessive traits in pea plants.

tossups.p: This scientist read his most famous paper aloud at two meetings of the Natural History Society of Brünn, the German name for Brno, in 1865. In that paper, he described hidden units passed from parents to offspring, often called his “factors,” which were later named genes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Austrian monk who discovered the law of segregation by studying pea plants.

tossups.p: Besides plants, this scientist bred honeybees and kept careful weather records for years. In 1868 he became abbot of his monastery, and he spent much of his later life fighting a government tax on monasteries.
tossups.r: His work was rediscovered in 1900. For 10 points, name this monk whose crosses of pea plants revealed the laws of heredity.

tossups.p: Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri [“boh-VAIR-ee”] explained this scientist’s results in the early 1900s by proposing that his hereditary units are carried on chromosomes. Working before chromosomes were understood, he concluded that each parent passes on only one of its two copies of each unit.
tossups.r: That idea is his law of segregation. For 10 points, name this monk who studied heredity in pea plants.

tossups.p: This scientist was born to a farming family in Austrian Silesia [“sye-LEE-zhuh”] in 1822 and took a new first name when he entered an Augustinian monastery in 1843. He later taught science at a school in Brno.
tossups.r: Crossing hybrids, he found a 3 to 1 ratio of dominant to recessive traits. For 10 points, name this “father of genetics” who experimented on pea plants.

tossups.p: This scientist tracked seven traits, including whether pods were inflated or pinched and whether flowers grew along the stem or at its tip. His plant was a good choice because it grows quickly, has clear either-or traits, and normally pollinates itself.
tossups.r: He worked in a monastery garden in Brno. For 10 points, name this monk who discovered the law of independent assortment.

tossups.p: To control which plants were crossed, this scientist snipped the pollen-making parts off flowers and dusted them with pollen from other plants. Crossing true-breeding tall and short plants, he found that all of the offspring were tall, but short plants reappeared in the next generation.
tossups.r: He called tall a dominant trait. For 10 points, name this Austrian monk who experimented on pea plants.

tossups.p: When this scientist followed seed shape and seed color at the same time, the second generation showed a ratio close to 9 to 3 to 3 to 1. Round, yellow seeds were the most common result.
tossups.r: That result supported his law of independent assortment. For 10 points, name this monk who bred pea plants in his monastery garden.

tossups.p: This scientist’s paper “Experiments on Plant Hybridization” described crosses of the plant Pisum sativum. In it, he called a trait that is hidden in hybrids “recessive” and the trait that shows “dominant.”
tossups.r: His work was rediscovered in 1900, long after his death in 1884. For 10 points, name this monk known as the “father of genetics.”

tossups.p: Reginald Punnett later invented a grid-shaped diagram for predicting the results of crosses like the ones this scientist performed. This scientist’s law of segregation says that the two copies of a hereditary unit separate when a parent makes reproductive cells.
tossups.r: He is often called the father of genetics. For 10 points, name this monk who crossbred pea plants.

tossups.p: From 1856 to 1863, this scientist grew and studied tens of thousands of plants in a garden at his monastery. He counted the offspring of each cross and used simple math to find patterns, an unusual approach for biology at the time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this monk who discovered the basic rules of heredity using pea plants.

tossups.p: This scientist’s work was ignored during his lifetime and rediscovered in 1900, 16 years after his death. He described traits as dominant or recessive and worked out the law of segregation by crossing plants in a monastery garden.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Austrian monk, called the “father of genetics,” who experimented on pea plants.

Following seed shape and seed color together gave a 9 to 3 to 3 to 1 ratio

Lived at St. Thomas’s Abbey in Brno, in the modern Czech Republic

Read “Experiments on Plant Hybridization” to the Natural History Society of Brünn (Brno) in 1865; it was published in 1866

Also bred honeybees and kept careful weather records
