trap.title: The monk, or his peas?
trap.body: Some tossups describe this man’s famous experiments but ask for the plant he used: peas, or Pisum sativum. Others want an idea that grew out of his work, like the law of segregation, or the Punnett square, which Reginald Punnett invented later. And his name sounds a lot like Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who made the periodic table.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This scientist,” “this monk,” or “this man” means Mendel; “this plant” or “this legume” means peas; “this law” or “this diagram” means the idea itself. Mendeleev clues are about chemistry and elements, not plants.
trap.line: Real answer line: Gregor Mendel (accept Gregor Johann Mendel; do not accept “Mendeleev”)

topics.name: Louis Pasteur
topics.kicker: French chemist and microbiologist · Pasteurization and the rabies vaccine
topics.briefing: Louis Pasteur was a French chemist who helped prove that tiny living microbes make food spoil and spread many diseases. A gentle heating method named for him, pasteurization, is still used to keep milk safe, and his lab created vaccines against anthrax and rabies. In 1885 his rabies shots saved a nine-year-old boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog, even though Pasteur was not a medical doctor.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a young chemist, this man used tweezers to separate tiny mirror-image crystals of a tartaric acid salt, and he found that solutions of the two kinds twisted polarized light in opposite directions. That work showed that molecules can be left- or right-handed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French scientist who later made a rabies vaccine and has a milk-heating process named for him.

tossups.p: While serving as dean of the science faculty at Lille, this scientist declared that “chance favors only the prepared mind.” Later, a local businessman asked him why the alcohol he made from beet juice kept turning sour, which led him to study fermentation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French scientist who showed that microbes cause fermentation and developed a rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: This scientist won a famous argument with Félix Pouchet [“poo-SHAY”] by boiling broth in flasks with long, curved necks that let air in but trapped dust and microbes. The broth stayed clear unless a flask’s neck was broken off, disproving the idea of spontaneous generation.
tossups.r: A process named for him heats milk to kill germs. For 10 points, name this French scientist who also made vaccines against anthrax and rabies.

tossups.p: This scientist argued against Justus von Liebig [“LEE-big”], who believed fermentation was a purely chemical process. He showed instead that living yeast turns sugar into alcohol, and that other microbes can sour wine and beer. His book _Studies on Wine_ explained how to keep those microbes from spoiling wine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French scientist whose name is attached to a heating process that keeps milk safe.

tossups.p: An effect named for this scientist describes how oxygen slows down fermentation by yeast. Studying a fermentation that makes butyric [“byoo-TEER-ik”] acid, he found microbes that could live without any oxygen at all and were even harmed by it.
tossups.r: He also developed a rabies vaccine. For 10 points, name this French scientist who disproved spontaneous generation with swan-neck flasks.

tossups.p: From 1865 to 1870, this scientist helped save France’s silk industry by finding ways to stop silkworm diseases, including one called pébrine [“pay-BREEN”]. He had farmers check moths under a microscope and keep only the eggs of healthy ones.
tossups.r: A method of heating milk is named after him. For 10 points, name this French scientist who created the first rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: After a summer break, this scientist’s team injected chickens with an old culture of chicken cholera bacteria, and the birds survived. Those weakened bacteria then protected the chickens against fresh, deadly bacteria, showing that weakened germs could be used as vaccines.
tossups.r: He also disproved spontaneous generation. For 10 points, name this French scientist who later made a rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: In 1881 at Pouilly-le-Fort [“poo-YEE luh FOR”], this scientist vaccinated about half of a flock of sheep against anthrax and then exposed the whole flock to the disease. The vaccinated sheep survived, while the unvaccinated ones died, in a public test that made him famous.
tossups.r: A heating process for milk is named for him. For 10 points, name this French scientist who also developed a rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: This scientist and Émile Roux [“ROO”] weakened a deadly germ by drying pieces of spinal cord from infected rabbits. In 1885, a series of shots made this way saved nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog.
tossups.r: He was a chemist, not a medical doctor. For 10 points, name this French scientist who made the first rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: This scientist suggested that all treatments using weakened germs be called “vaccines,” to honor Edward Jenner’s use of cowpox, since the Latin word for cow is vacca. His own team made vaccines against chicken cholera and anthrax.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French scientist who made the first rabies vaccine and disproved spontaneous generation.

tossups.p: A stroke in 1868 left this scientist partly paralyzed on his left side, but he kept working for many more years, relying on assistants such as Charles Chamberland [“shahm-ber-LAHN”] for lab work. He was in the middle of studying silkworm diseases when the stroke hit.
tossups.r: A milk-heating process is named for him. For 10 points, name this French scientist who developed vaccines for anthrax and rabies.

tossups.p: Born in Dole in 1822 and raised in Arbois [“ar-BWAH”], this son of a tanner made skilled pastel portraits of his parents and neighbors as a teenager. He went on to study chemistry at the École Normale Supérieure [“ay-KOHL nor-MAHL soo-pay-RYUR”] in Paris.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French scientist who disproved spontaneous generation and made a rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: This scientist is buried in a decorated crypt beneath the Paris research institute named for him, which opened in 1888. Joseph Meister, the boy whose life this scientist saved, later worked at that institute as a caretaker.
tossups.r: He also showed that microbes cause fermentation. For 10 points, name this French scientist who made the first rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: Joseph Lister began using carbolic acid to clean wounds after reading this scientist’s work on microbes, and he later wrote to thank him. This scientist had a bitter rivalry with the German scientist Robert Koch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this French chemist who helped prove the germ theory of disease and made a rabies vaccine.

tossups.p: This scientist showed that gently heating wine kills the microbes that make it spoil, a process named for him that was later used on milk and juice. He also disproved spontaneous generation using flasks with curved necks.
tossups.r: He also helped prove the germ theory of disease. For 10 points, name this French scientist who created the first rabies vaccine.

clues.t: French chemist and microbiologist who helped prove the germ theory of disease
A gentle heating process that kills microbes in wine, milk, and juice is named for him
Made the first rabies vaccine; in 1885 it saved Joseph Meister, a boy bitten by a rabid dog
Disproved spontaneous generation using swan-neck flasks
The flasks’ long, curved necks let air in but trapped dust and microbes, so the boiled broth stayed clear
Showed that fermentation is caused by living yeast and other microbes, not just chemistry
As a young chemist, separated mirror-image crystals of a tartaric acid salt by hand; their solutions twisted polarized light in opposite directions
An old, weakened culture of chicken cholera bacteria protected chickens, showing that weakened germs can work as vaccines
Publicly tested an anthrax vaccine on sheep at Pouilly-le-Fort in 1881
A research institute named for him opened in Paris in 1888; he is buried in a crypt there
Saved France’s silk industry (1865–1870) by fighting silkworm diseases such as pébrine
Had a bitter rivalry with the German scientist Robert Koch
Joseph Lister used his ideas about microbes to develop antiseptic surgery with carbolic acid
Said that “chance favors only the prepared mind”
As dean of science at Lille, studied why alcohol made from beet juice kept turning sour
Won his spontaneous generation debate against Félix Pouchet
Argued against Justus von Liebig, who thought fermentation was purely chemical
An effect named for him describes how oxygen slows down fermentation by yeast
Studying butyric acid fermentation, found microbes that live without oxygen and are even harmed by it
Described the diseases of wine and how to prevent them in his book _Studies on Wine_
Assistants Émile Roux and Charles Chamberland helped develop his vaccines
Weakened the rabies germ by drying pieces of spinal cord from infected rabbits
Proposed calling all weakened-germ treatments “vaccines” to honor Edward Jenner’s cowpox work (Latin vacca, “cow”)
A stroke in 1868 left him partly paralyzed on his left side, but he kept working
Born in Dole in 1822 and raised in Arbois, the son of a tanner; drew skilled pastel portraits as a teenager
Studied chemistry at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris
Joseph Meister, the boy his rabies shots saved, later worked as a caretaker at the institute named for him

trap.title: Pasteur, Koch, or Lister?
trap.body: Several scientists built the germ theory of disease, and their clues blur together. Robert Koch, a German doctor, proved that specific bacteria cause anthrax, tuberculosis, and cholera, and wrote Koch’s postulates, so anthrax shows up in both men’s clues. Joseph Lister, a British surgeon, used carbolic acid to keep wounds clean after reading Pasteur’s work, and Edward Jenner made the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796.
trap.fix: Pasteur clues are about chemistry and France: mirror-image crystals, fermentation, swan-neck flasks, a heating process named for him, and the rabies vaccine. Postulates, tuberculosis, and Germany mean Koch; surgery and carbolic acid mean Lister; cowpox and smallpox mean Jenner.

topics.name: Lysosomes
topics.kicker: Organelles full of digestive enzymes · The cell’s cleanup and recycling crew
topics.dates: Named by Christian de Duve in 1955
topics.briefing: Lysosomes are the cell’s cleanup and recycling crew: small, bubble-like organelles packed with dozens of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out cell parts, food particles, and invading bacteria. Their insides are kept acidic, and their enzymes work best in acid, which helps protect the rest of the cell if one leaks. Belgian scientist Christian de Duve discovered them in the 1950s and later shared a Nobel Prize.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Christian de Duve [“duh DOOV”] found this organelle after noticing that an enzyme called acid phosphatase became more active when rat liver samples sat in a refrigerator for several days, because the membranes holding the enzyme slowly broke open. He named this organelle in 1955.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these organelles full of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out cell parts.

tossups.p: Alex Novikoff took the first electron microscope pictures of this organelle in 1955, working with its discoverer, Christian de Duve [“duh DOOV”]. Its interior is kept at a pH of about 4.5 to 5 by pumps that bring in hydrogen ions.
tossups.r: Plants mostly rely on vacuoles for its job instead. For 10 points, name this organelle that uses digestive enzymes to break down old cell parts.

tossups.p: Enzymes bound for this organelle are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate [“MAN-ohs six FOSS-fate”] in the Golgi apparatus. In I-cell disease, that tag is never added, so the enzymes are shipped out of the cell instead and undigested material piles up.
tossups.r: It is nicknamed the cell’s recycling center. For 10 points, name this acidic organelle that digests worn-out cell parts and invading bacteria.

tossups.p: Yoshinori Ohsumi [“oh-SOO-mee”] won the 2016 Nobel Prize for his work on autophagy, a “self-eating” process in which animal cells wrap up their own worn-out parts and deliver them to this organelle. Its enzymes then break those parts down so their building blocks can be reused.
tossups.r: Its enzymes are shipped to it by the Golgi apparatus. For 10 points, name this organelle, nicknamed the cell’s recycling center.

tossups.p: As a tadpole turns into a frog, enzymes from this organelle help break down its tail, which shrinks away. Those enzymes, called acid hydrolases [“HY-druh-lay-zez”], work best at a low pH, so they do little damage if they leak into the cytoplasm.
tossups.r: Plants use vacuoles for much of this job. For 10 points, name this organelle that digests food particles and old cell parts.

tossups.p: Pompe [“POM-puh”] disease, a glycogen storage disease, and Gaucher [“go-SHAY”] disease both happen when this organelle is missing one of its enzymes. In Tay-Sachs disease, a missing enzyme in this organelle lets a fatty substance build up in nerve cells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle that uses digestive enzymes to break down materials inside the cell.

tossups.p: Bone-dissolving cells called osteoclasts [“OSS-tee-oh-klasts”] release enzymes from this organelle, along with acid, to break down old bone. This organelle’s enzymes work best at a pH of about 5, which is much more acidic than the rest of the cell.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle filled with digestive enzymes that breaks down worn-out cell parts.

tossups.p: Protein-cutting enzymes called cathepsins [“kuh-THEP-sinz”] do much of their work inside this organelle, alongside dozens of other enzymes that break down fats, sugars, and nucleic acids. Its enzymes are made on the rough ER and delivered by way of the Golgi apparatus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle, the cell’s main digestive compartment, found mostly in animal cells.

tossups.p: Albert Claude and George Palade [“puh-LAH-day”] shared the 1974 Nobel Prize with the Belgian scientist who discovered this organelle. That scientist, Christian de Duve, also discovered peroxisomes, which break down hydrogen peroxide, while this organelle uses acid-loving digestive enzymes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle that breaks down worn-out cell parts, food particles, and bacteria.

tossups.p: Older textbooks call a newly formed one of these organelles “primary” and one that has fused with material to digest “secondary.” Material that a cell takes in by endocytosis passes through compartments called endosomes before reaching this organelle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle that uses digestive enzymes to break down worn-out cell parts.

tossups.p: A pump called a V-type ATPase uses energy from ATP to push hydrogen ions into this organelle, keeping its inside acidic. This organelle’s name comes from Greek words meaning “loosening” and “body,” and plant cells mostly let their large central vacuole do its job.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle, found mainly in animal cells, that is packed with digestive enzymes.

tossups.p: When cells die, enzymes leaking out of this organelle help digest them in a process called autolysis [“aw-TOL-ih-sis”], or self-digestion. In living cells, this organelle breaks down worn-out mitochondria and other old parts so their materials can be reused.
tossups.r: It is found mainly in animal cells. For 10 points, name this organelle, the cell’s cleanup crew, packed with digestive enzymes.

tossups.p: When a white blood cell swallows a bacterium, the bacterium ends up inside a sac called a phagosome, which then fuses with this organelle so its enzymes can destroy the invader. Single-celled organisms like amoebas digest their food the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle, sometimes called the cell’s recycling center, that is full of digestive enzymes.

tossups.p: This organelle should not be confused with a similarly named enzyme in tears and saliva that Alexander Fleming discovered. This organelle’s own enzymes include nucleases, lipases, and proteases, which break down nucleic acids, fats, and proteins.
tossups.r: Its inside is kept acidic. For 10 points, name this organelle that breaks down worn-out cell parts.

tossups.p: This organelle is a small sac wrapped in a single membrane and filled with dozens of digestive enzymes. It breaks down food particles, invading bacteria, and worn-out cell parts, and it is found mainly in animal cells.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle often called the cell’s garbage disposal or recycling center.

clues.t: Small, membrane-bound organelles filled with dozens of digestive enzymes

Sometimes nicknamed “suicide bags,” because their enzymes could break down the cell if many of them burst at once
Found mainly in animal cells; plant cells mostly use their large central vacuole for the same job
Their enzymes are made on the rough ER and delivered by way of the Golgi apparatus
Kept acidic inside (about pH 4.5 to 5) by V-type ATPase pumps that push in hydrogen ions
Their enzymes, called acid hydrolases, work best in acid, so a leak into the neutral cytoplasm does little harm
White blood cells destroy swallowed bacteria when a phagosome fuses with one of these; amoebas digest food this way too
In autophagy (“self-eating”), worn-out cell parts are wrapped up and delivered to them for recycling
Tay-Sachs disease happens when one of their enzymes is missing, so a fatty substance builds up in nerve cells
Discovered by Belgian scientist Christian de Duve, who named them in 1955
Material taken in by endocytosis passes through endosomes on its way to them
When cells die, their leaking enzymes help digest the cells in autolysis (self-digestion)
De Duve noticed that acid phosphatase became more active after rat liver samples sat in a refrigerator for days, as the membranes around it broke
Alex Novikoff took the first electron microscope pictures of them in 1955
De Duve shared the 1974 Nobel Prize with Albert Claude and George Palade
De Duve also discovered peroxisomes, a different organelle that breaks down hydrogen peroxide
Enzymes headed for them get a mannose-6-phosphate tag in the Golgi apparatus
In I-cell disease that tag is missing, so the enzymes are shipped out of the cell instead
Gaucher disease and Pompe disease (a glycogen storage disease) also come from missing enzymes here
Yoshinori Ohsumi won the 2016 Nobel Prize for his work on autophagy
As a tadpole turns into a frog, their enzymes help break down its shrinking tail
Protein-cutting enzymes called cathepsins work inside them, alongside nucleases and lipases
Bone-dissolving osteoclasts release enzymes from them, along with acid, to break down old bone
Older textbooks call new ones “primary” and ones that have fused with material to digest “secondary”
The name comes from Greek words meaning “loosening” and “body”

trap.title: Lysosome or lysozyme?
trap.body: Lysozyme sounds almost the same, but it is a single enzyme in tears and saliva that breaks open bacterial cell walls, discovered by Alexander Fleming, not an organelle. Peroxisomes are a different organelle, also discovered by Christian de Duve, that destroy hydrogen peroxide. And plant cells mostly let their large central vacuole do the lysosome’s cleanup job.
trap.fix: If the clues mention acid hydrolases, autophagy, Tay-Sachs disease, or mannose-6-phosphate, say lysosome. Hydrogen peroxide and the enzyme catalase mean peroxisome; tears and Fleming mean lysozyme.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lysosomes (accept lysosome; do not accept “lysozyme” or “peroxisome”)

topics.name: Golgi apparatus
topics.kicker: Stacked membrane sacs that finish proteins · The cell’s post office
topics.briefing: The Golgi apparatus is the cell’s shipping department: a stack of flattened, pancake-like membrane sacs that receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, finishes them by adding sugars and other tags, and sorts them into little bubbles called vesicles. Those vesicles carry each package to where it belongs, whether that is a lysosome, the cell membrane, or the outside of the cell. Italian scientist Camillo Golgi first described it in 1898.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A silver-staining method called the “black reaction” let a scientist discover this structure inside nerve cells in 1898. That scientist shared the 1906 Nobel Prize with Santiago Ramón y Cajal [“kah-HAHL”], even though the two disagreed about how neurons connect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle, named after its Italian discoverer, that packages proteins into vesicles.

tossups.p: For decades after its discovery, many scientists thought this structure was just a mistake caused by staining, until electron microscopes showed it clearly in the 1950s. Under those microscopes, it looks like a curved stack of flattened sacs called cisternae [“sis-TER-nee”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle that sorts and ships proteins made in the endoplasmic reticulum.

tossups.p: Vesicles coated with a protein complex called COPII [“cop two”] carry cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum to this organelle, while COPI-coated vesicles carry escaped proteins back the other way. Its receiving side is called the cis face, and its shipping side is called the trans face.
tossups.r: It is nicknamed the cell’s post office. For 10 points, name this stack of membrane sacs that packages proteins for delivery.

tossups.p: George Palade [“puh-LAH-day”] tracked radioactive amino acids through pancreas cells in pulse-chase experiments. He showed that newly made proteins travel from the rough ER to this organelle and then into secretory granules that release them from the cell.
tossups.r: Cells that release lots of protein have especially large versions of it. For 10 points, name this organelle, nicknamed the cell’s post office.

tossups.p: A fungal chemical called brefeldin [“breh-FELL-din”] A makes this organelle fall apart and merge back into the endoplasmic reticulum. Normally, proteins enter this organelle at its cis face, get modified as they pass through its stacked sacs, and leave from its trans face.
tossups.r: It is named for an Italian scientist. For 10 points, name this organelle that packages proteins into vesicles.

tossups.p: Proteins that belong in the endoplasmic reticulum end in a tag of four amino acids, written K-D-E-L, so if they drift into this organelle, receptors catch them and send them back. This organelle adds sugar chains to many other proteins, turning them into glycoproteins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this stack of flattened sacs that sorts proteins and ships them in vesicles.

tossups.p: James Rothman, Randy Schekman, and Thomas Südhof [“SOOD-hof”] won the 2013 Nobel Prize for discovering how cells move cargo in vesicles, like the ones that travel to and from this organelle. Schekman found key genes for that traffic by studying mutant yeast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle, made of flattened membrane sacs, that modifies and packages proteins.

tossups.p: Scientists long debated two models of how cargo moves through this organelle: in one, vesicles hop between fixed sacs, and in the other, called cisternal maturation, each sac slowly changes as it moves through the stack. Either way, products leave from its trans face.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle that receives proteins from the ER and ships them out in vesicles.

tossups.p: This organelle attaches O-linked sugar chains to the amino acids serine and threonine, and it trims and reshapes sugar chains that were added earlier in the ER. It also tags enzymes bound for lysosomes with mannose-6-phosphate [“MAN-ohs six FOSS-fate”].
tossups.r: Its products leave in vesicles. For 10 points, name this stack of membrane sacs, nicknamed the cell’s post office.

tossups.p: When an animal cell divides, this organelle breaks into many small pieces that are shared between the two daughter cells, where they reassemble. In animal cells, this organelle usually sits close to the nucleus, near the centrosome.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organelle that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum.

tossups.p: This organelle makes pectin and hemicellulose for plant cell walls, although cellulose itself is made at the cell membrane. In dividing plant cells, vesicles from this organelle gather at the middle of the cell and fuse to form the cell plate.
tossups.r: It is nicknamed the cell’s post office. For 10 points, name this organelle that packages proteins and other molecules into vesicles.

tossups.p: Vesicles coated with the protein clathrin [“CLATH-rin”] bud from the trans side of this organelle, carrying digestive enzymes to lysosomes. Other vesicles from this organelle fuse with the cell membrane and release their contents outside the cell by exocytosis.
tossups.r: It is made of stacked, flattened sacs. For 10 points, name this organelle that receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum.

tossups.p: Mucus-making goblet cells in the intestines and antibody-making plasma cells both have especially large versions of this organelle, because they release so much material. Its products are sealed into vesicles that later fuse with the cell membrane.
tossups.r: It receives proteins from the ER. For 10 points, name this organelle, nicknamed the cell’s post office or shipping center.

tossups.p: A sorting web of tubes and vesicles sits on the trans, or shipping, side of this organelle and sends each piece of cargo to the right place. This organelle is part of the endomembrane system, along with the endoplasmic reticulum, lysosomes, and the cell membrane.
tossups.r: It packages proteins into vesicles. For 10 points, name this stack of flattened sacs named for an Italian scientist.

tossups.p: This organelle is a stack of flattened membrane sacs that receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, finishes them by adding sugars and other tags, and sorts them by destination. It then ships them out in small bubbles called vesicles.
tossups.r: It is named for an Italian scientist. For 10 points, name this organelle, often called the cell’s post office.

clues.t: A stack of flattened membrane sacs, usually near the nucleus
Modifies, sorts, and packages proteins it receives from the endoplasmic reticulum
Ships its finished products out in small bubbles called vesicles
Nicknamed the cell’s post office or shipping department
Named for the Italian scientist who discovered it in 1898
Each flattened sac in the stack is called a cisterna (plural cisternae)
Has a cis (receiving) face toward the ER and a trans (shipping) face, where a web of tubes and vesicles sorts cargo
Adds and trims sugar chains on proteins, turning them into glycoproteins
Sends digestive enzymes to lysosomes
Extra large in cells that secrete a lot, like mucus-making goblet cells and antibody-making plasma cells
In dividing plant cells, its vesicles gather to build the cell plate between the two new cells
Makes plant cell-wall materials such as pectin and hemicellulose, but not cellulose, which is made at the cell membrane
Part of the endomembrane system, along with the ER, lysosomes, and the cell membrane
Some of its vesicles fuse with the cell membrane and release their contents outside the cell, in exocytosis
Its discoverer found it inside nerve cells using a silver-staining method called the “black reaction”
Its discoverer shared the 1906 Nobel Prize with Santiago Ramón y Cajal, though they disagreed about how neurons connect
Many scientists thought it was a staining mistake until electron microscopes showed it clearly in the 1950s
COPII-coated vesicles bring cargo to it from the ER; COPI-coated vesicles carry escaped proteins back
Clathrin-coated vesicles leave its trans side carrying enzymes bound for lysosomes
Tags enzymes headed for lysosomes with mannose-6-phosphate
George Palade’s pulse-chase experiments on pancreas cells traced new proteins from the rough ER through it to secretory granules
In the cisternal maturation model, each sac slowly changes as it moves through the stack, instead of cargo hopping between fixed sacs
A fungal chemical called brefeldin A makes it fall apart and merge back into the ER
ER proteins ending in the amino acid tag K-D-E-L are caught here and sent back to the ER
James Rothman, Randy Schekman, and Thomas Südhof won the 2013 Nobel Prize for discovering how cells move cargo in vesicles
Attaches O-linked sugar chains to the amino acids serine and threonine
Breaks into small pieces when an animal cell divides, then reassembles in each daughter cell; usually sits near the centrosome

trap.title: Golgi or the ER?
trap.body: The endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus work as a team, so their clues blur together. The rough ER, studded with ribosomes, makes proteins; the Golgi receives them at its cis face, modifies them, and ships them out from its trans face in vesicles. Players who hear “proteins,” “vesicles,” “cisternae,” or the K-D-E-L tag, which turn up in both organelles’ tossups, often buzz with the wrong one.
trap.fix: A stack of flattened sacs with cis and trans faces, sorting, packaging, and “post office” mean Golgi. Ribosomes on the surface, a network connected to the nuclear envelope, or making lipids mean the ER. If a question asks for the Italian scientist himself, say Camillo Golgi.
trap.line: Real answer line: Golgi apparatus (accept Golgi body or Golgi complex; accept dictyosomes)

topics.name: RNA
topics.kicker: Single-stranded nucleic acid with uracil · Turns genes into proteins
topics.briefing: RNA is DNA’s single-stranded chemical cousin, and it does a surprising amount of the cell’s work. Messenger RNA carries copies of genes from DNA to the ribosomes, transfer RNA brings the matching amino acids, and ribosomal RNA helps link those amino acids into proteins. It uses the sugar ribose and the base uracil in place of thymine, and many viruses, including flu viruses, store their genes in it.
topics.answerHtml: RNA (or ribonucleic acid; prompt on nucleic acid; do not accept “DNA” or one specific type such as “mRNA”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1986, Walter Gilbert named a hypothesis proposing that early life used this molecule both to store genetic information and to speed up chemical reactions. That idea grew out of discoveries by Thomas Cech [“CHECK”] and Sidney Altman that some molecules of this kind act as enzymes, called ribozymes.
tossups.r: It is usually single-stranded. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that uses uracil instead of thymine.

tossups.p: In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei cracked the first codon by adding a synthetic chain of this molecule whose bases were all uracil to a cell extract. The extract then built a protein chain made only of the amino acid phenylalanine.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.

tossups.p: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello won the 2006 Nobel Prize for discovering that double-stranded pieces of this molecule can silence matching genes in worms, a process called interference. Short “micro” versions of this molecule control genes in a similar way.
tossups.r: It uses uracil instead of thymine. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that contains the sugar ribose.

tossups.p: Katalin Karikó [“KAH-ree-koh”] and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize for showing that changing one of this molecule’s bases keeps it from setting off an unwanted immune reaction. That work made possible the COVID-19 vaccines built from this molecule’s messenger type.
tossups.r: It is made from DNA by transcription. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that uses ribose and uracil.

tossups.p: Scientists detect this molecule with a lab method called the Northern blot, named as a play on the Southern blot, which detects DNA and was named for Edwin Southern. This molecule is less stable than DNA because its sugar carries an extra hydroxyl group.
tossups.r: It contains uracil. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that comes in messenger, transfer, and ribosomal types.

tossups.p: Viroids, tiny plant pathogens first identified by Theodor Diener in 1971, are nothing more than short circles of this molecule with no protein coat. Many viruses, including flu viruses and coronaviruses, also store their genes in this molecule instead of DNA.
tossups.r: It is usually single-stranded. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that uses uracil in place of thymine.

tossups.p: In 1977, Phillip Sharp and Richard Roberts discovered that many genes come in pieces. Before a copy of such a gene, made of this molecule, can be used, its introns must be cut out and its exons joined by spliceosomes.
tossups.r: Spliceosomes are built partly from small molecules of this kind. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid made from DNA during transcription.

tossups.p: In CRISPR gene editing, a guide made of this molecule leads the Cas9 [“kass nine”] enzyme to the exact spot in DNA that it should cut. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier [“shar-pahn-TYAY”] won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing that tool.
tossups.r: It is usually single-stranded. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that contains ribose and uracil.

tossups.p: An enzyme called primase lays down short primers of this molecule so that DNA polymerase can start copying DNA, including at the start of each Okazaki [“oh-kah-ZAH-kee”] fragment. Those primers are later removed and replaced with DNA.
tossups.r: It uses uracil instead of thymine. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid whose messenger type carries genes to ribosomes.

tossups.p: In 1965, Robert Holley worked out the complete sequence of one transfer type of this molecule, taken from yeast. That type of this molecule folds into a cloverleaf shape and uses a three-base anticodon to carry the right amino acid to the ribosome.
tossups.r: It contains uracil. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that also has messenger and ribosomal types.

tossups.p: In eukaryotes, the messenger type of this molecule gets a protective cap on its five-prime end and a long poly-A tail of adenine nucleotides on its three-prime end before leaving the nucleus. This molecule is built in the five-prime to three-prime direction during transcription.
tossups.r: It is usually single-stranded. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that uses uracil instead of thymine.

tossups.p: Howard Temin and David Baltimore each discovered reverse transcriptase in 1970, an enzyme that copies this molecule back into DNA. Retroviruses such as HIV use that enzyme because their genes are stored in this molecule.
tossups.r: It contains the sugar ribose. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that is made from DNA during transcription.

tossups.p: Francis Crick’s “central dogma” says that genetic information flows from DNA to this molecule and then to protein. In the second step, ribosomes read this molecule’s messenger type three bases at a time, in units called codons.
tossups.r: It is usually single-stranded. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that uses uracil instead of thymine.

tossups.p: The lab of Severo Ochoa [“oh-CHOH-uh”] found an enzyme that could build chains of this molecule in a test tube, helping him win a share of the 1959 Nobel Prize. Pictures of the ribosome later showed that its amino-acid–linking center is made of this molecule, not protein.
tossups.r: It is made from DNA by transcription. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that contains uracil and ribose.

tossups.p: This molecule is usually single-stranded, uses the sugar ribose, and has the base uracil in place of thymine. It is made from a DNA template during transcription and comes in messenger, transfer, and ribosomal types.
tossups.r: Ribosomes read its messenger type. For 10 points, name this nucleic acid that helps cells turn genes into proteins.

clues.t: Uses the base uracil in place of thymine
Its sugar is ribose, which has one more oxygen atom than DNA’s sugar, deoxyribose
Usually single-stranded, unlike the double helix of DNA
Made from a DNA template during transcription
Comes in three main types: messenger, transfer, and ribosomal
The messenger type carries a gene’s code to the ribosomes in three-base “words” called codons
The cloverleaf-shaped transfer type uses a three-base anticodon to bring the right amino acid
The ribosomal type, along with proteins, makes up the ribosomes
Ribosomes read the messenger type to build proteins in translation
Francis Crick’s “central dogma”: genetic information flows from DNA to this molecule to protein
Spliceosomes cut out introns and join exons together in a step called splicing
Flu viruses, coronaviruses, and HIV store their genes in it instead of DNA
Retroviruses like HIV copy it into DNA with reverse transcriptase, found by Howard Temin and David Baltimore in 1970
Some molecules of it act as enzymes called ribozymes; the ribosome’s amino-acid–linking center is one
Less stable than DNA, because the extra hydroxyl group on its sugar helps it break apart
In 1986, Walter Gilbert named the hypothesis that early life used it both to store genes and to speed up reactions
Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman won the 1989 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing it can act as an enzyme
In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei cracked the first codon: a chain whose bases were all uracil built a chain of phenylalanine
Robert Holley worked out the full sequence of a transfer type from yeast in 1965
Andrew Fire and Craig Mello won the 2006 Nobel Prize for discovering gene-silencing “interference” in worms
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 Nobel Prize for base changes that made messenger-type COVID-19 vaccines possible
Detected with the Northern blot, named as a play on the Southern blot for DNA
Severo Ochoa’s lab found an enzyme that builds chains of it in a test tube; Ochoa shared the 1959 Nobel Prize
Viroids, plant pathogens identified by Theodor Diener in 1971, are short circles of it with no protein coat
Phillip Sharp and Richard Roberts discovered in 1977 that many genes come in pieces that must be spliced
Primase makes short primers of it to start DNA copying, including each Okazaki fragment
In eukaryotes, the messenger type gets a five-prime cap and a three-prime poly-A tail before leaving the nucleus
In CRISPR gene editing, a guide made of it leads Cas9 to its target; Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry

trap.title: RNA, DNA, or one type?
trap.body: RNA and DNA are both nucleic acids built from nucleotides, so players mix them up, especially on clues about sugars and bases. RNA uses ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded; DNA uses deoxyribose and thymine and forms a double helix. Some tossups also ask for one specific type, like messenger RNA or transfer RNA, instead of RNA in general.
trap.fix: Uracil, ribose, ribozymes, or a single strand mean RNA; thymine, deoxyribose, or a double helix mean DNA. Say just “RNA” when a question asks for “this nucleic acid” or “this molecule,” and name a type only when it asks for “this type of RNA,” such as the one with codons (mRNA) or the one with anticodons (tRNA).
trap.line: Real answer line: RNA (or ribonucleic acid; prompt on nucleic acid; do not accept “DNA” or one specific type such as “mRNA”)

topics.name: Xylem
topics.kicker: Plant tissue that carries water up from the roots · Wood is made of it
topics.briefing: Xylem is a plant’s plumbing: tubes of tough, dead, hollow cells that carry water and minerals from the roots up to the leaves. As water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls the column of water behind it upward, lifting water more than 100 meters to the tops of the tallest redwoods. Wood is mostly xylem, and a tree’s rings are layers of it added year after year.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli [“NAY-guh-lee”] named this tissue in 1858 from the Greek word for “wood.” In a tree trunk, the vascular cambium adds a new layer of this tissue each year, forming growth rings that can be counted to find the tree’s age.
tossups.r: It works alongside phloem. For 10 points, name this plant tissue that carries water up from the roots.

tossups.p: Henry Dixon and John Joly [“JOH-lee”] proposed in the 1890s that water is pulled up this tissue as one unbroken column, held together because water molecules cling to one another. In their cohesion-tension theory, the pull comes from water evaporating out of leaves through tiny pores called stomata.
tossups.r: It can lift water more than 100 meters up the tallest redwoods. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue, which works alongside phloem.

tossups.p: In his 1727 book _Vegetable Staticks_, Stephen Hales measured how much water plants lose through their leaves and how strongly their roots push water upward. That push, called root pressure, can force water up this tissue and out of leaf edges as droplets, a process called guttation [“guh-TAY-shun”].
tossups.r: Phloem works alongside it. For 10 points, name this plant tissue made of tracheids and vessel elements.

tossups.p: In flowering plants, cells called vessel elements are stacked end to end and joined by openings called perforation plates, forming long, open pipes in this tissue. Narrower, tapered cells called tracheids [“TRAY-kee-idz”] also carry water through this tissue.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that moves water and minerals up from a plant’s roots.

tossups.p: Conifer wood is made almost entirely of cells called tracheids, which pass water to one another through thin spots called pits; in many conifers, each pit has a valve-like plug called a torus. Those cells belong to this tissue, which also includes the wider vessels of flowering trees.
tossups.r: It works with phloem. For 10 points, name this plant tissue that carries water upward from the roots.

tossups.p: Balloon-like growths called tyloses [“tye-LOH-seez”] plug the old vessels of this tissue in white oak, making that wood watertight enough to hold liquid in barrels. In a tree trunk, the heartwood at the center is made of old layers of this tissue that no longer carry water.
tossups.r: It carries water up from the roots. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue whose outer, working layers form the sapwood.

tossups.p: A bacterium that causes Pierce’s disease in grapevines is spread by insects called sharpshooters and can kill vines by clogging this tissue. Dutch elm disease, caused by a fungus, can also kill trees by blocking water flow through this tissue.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plant tissue that carries water and minerals, unlike phloem, which carries sugar.

tossups.p: In late winter, the sugary sap that people collect from maple trees and boil down into syrup comes from this tissue. The sap flows best when freezing nights are followed by thawing days, which build up pressure inside the trunk.
tossups.r: Wood is made mostly of it. For 10 points, name this plant tissue that carries water and minerals up from the roots.

tossups.p: During droughts or hard freezes, air bubbles can form inside this tissue and break its water columns, a problem called cavitation or embolism. Plants survive this partly because water can detour sideways around a blocked cell through thin spots in the cell walls called pits.
tossups.r: Phloem works alongside it. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries water up from the roots.

tossups.p: Before water from the soil can enter this tissue in a root, it must pass through living cells at the Casparian [“kas-PAIR-ee-un”] strip, a waxy band in the endodermis. In the center of many roots, this tissue forms an X- or star-shaped core.
tossups.r: It works alongside phloem. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries water up to the leaves.

tossups.p: The first cells of this tissue to form in a young stem have ring- or spiral-shaped thickenings in their walls, which let them stretch as the stem grows longer. Later cells of this tissue have thicker walls stiffened with lignin.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this plant tissue that carries water and minerals up from the roots.

tossups.p: Vascular plants, also called tracheophytes, carry water through cells such as tracheids in this tissue. Mosses and other bryophytes lack this tissue, which is one reason they stay small and grow in damp places.
tossups.r: Wood is made mostly of it. For 10 points, name this water-carrying plant tissue that works alongside phloem.

tossups.p: In leaf veins, this tissue usually lies on the upper side, with phloem below it. If you stand a stalk of celery or a white carnation in colored water, the dye climbs through tubes of this tissue and tints the leaves or petals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that carries water and minerals up from the roots.

tossups.p: In a typical stem, this tissue sits on the inner side of each vascular bundle, with phloem on the outer side. As a tree trunk thickens, the vascular cambium adds new cells of this tissue toward the inside and new phloem toward the outside.
tossups.r: It carries water up from the roots. For 10 points, name this plant tissue that makes up wood.

tossups.p: This plant tissue is made mostly of dead, hollow cells with stiff walls that link up into tiny pipes. It carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots up to the leaves, pulled along as water evaporates from the leaves.
tossups.r: Wood is made mostly of it. For 10 points, name this vascular tissue that works alongside phloem.

One of the two vascular tissues, along with phloem, which carries sugar
Wood is mostly made of it, and tree rings are yearly layers of it
Its water-carrying cells are dead and hollow when they do their job
Water moves through it in one direction, upward, while phloem carries sugar both up and down
Made of two kinds of water-carrying cells: long, narrow tracheids and wider vessel elements
Its cell walls are stiffened with lignin, which also helps hold the plant up
Water evaporating from leaves (transpiration) pulls water up through it, as high as the tops of redwoods more than 100 meters tall
The cohesion-tension theory: hydrogen bonds hold the water column together as it is pulled up
Root pressure can push water up it and out of leaf edges as droplets, which is called guttation
The vascular cambium adds new layers of it toward the inside of a stem and new phloem toward the outside
Heartwood is old, non-working layers of it at a tree’s center; sapwood is the outer, working part
Celery stalks or white carnations stood in colored water show dye climbing up through it
Mosses and other bryophytes lack it, which helps keep them small; vascular plants are called tracheophytes
Runs with phloem in leaf veins and vascular bundles, usually on the upper side of a vein and the inner side of a bundle
Swiss botanist Carl Nägeli named it in 1858, from the Greek word for “wood”
Henry Dixon and John Joly proposed the cohesion-tension theory in the 1890s
Stephen Hales measured water loss and root pressure in his 1727 book _Vegetable Staticks_
Vessel elements are stacked end to end and joined by openings called perforation plates
Water passes sideways between its cells through thin spots called pits; many conifer pits have a valve-like plug called a torus
Conifer wood (softwood) is almost all tracheids; flowering trees (hardwoods) also have wide vessels
Air bubbles from drought or freezing can break its water columns, which is called cavitation or embolism
Balloon-like tyloses plug its old vessels; in white oak they make the wood watertight enough for barrels
The bacterium behind Pierce’s disease of grapevines, spread by sharpshooter insects, clogs it
Dutch elm disease, caused by a fungus, can kill trees by blocking water flow through it
The sugary maple sap that is boiled down into maple syrup in late winter comes from it; it flows best after freezing nights and thawing days
Its first-formed cells have ring- or spiral-shaped wall thickenings that let them stretch as the stem grows
Water must pass through living cells at the root’s Casparian strip, in the endodermis, before entering it

trap.title: Xylem or phloem?
trap.body: Xylem and phloem are the two vascular tissues, and tossups often mention both. Xylem carries water and minerals up from the roots and is made mostly of dead, hollow cells; phloem carries sugar from the leaves to the rest of the plant through living sieve-tube cells. The vascular cambium, which makes new xylem and phloem, is a third answer that players confuse with both.
trap.fix: Water, minerals, transpiration, tracheids, vessel elements, lignin, wood, or tree rings mean xylem. Sugar, sap flowing both up and down, sieve tubes, companion cells, or aphids mean phloem, except that the sugary sap tapped for maple syrup comes from xylem. A memory trick: phloem carries food.
trap.line: Real answer line: Xylem (prompt on vascular tissue; do not accept “phloem”)
